title: memory-fragmentation-oom-root-cause-notes
content:
Summary:

Notes from investigation into intermittent OOMs and suspected memory fragmentation on serving runtime instances (NVidia A100 / CUDA 11.8 baseline). Observed behavior: long-running model servers gradually hit OOM with no clear increase in concurrent request rate; GPU memory usage (as reported by nvidia-smi) shows free memory fluctuating and not reclaimed despite low live allocation counts.

Root hypotheses considered: 
- Allocator fragmentation in the CUDA driver / runtime (cudaMalloc/cudaFree) causing usable free memory to be fragmented into small pockets, preventing large contiguous allocations for transient workspaces.
- Our workspace sizing strategy requests different workspace sizes across model versions and sequence lengths causing a fragmented allocation pattern.
- cudaMallocSync/legacy cudaMalloc + host-side caching allocator interactions (e.g., caching layer returning small freed chunks leading to fragmentation).
- Persistent allocations from KV cache growth or pinned host buffers not being released due to bugs / reference leaks.
- Third-party libs (cuBLAS/cuDNN/cuSparse) performing internal workspace allocations that are not visible at the same abstraction level.

What we observed / evidence collected:
- Repro steps: left a dedicated capacity instance running the latest small-llm model under low qps (~1 rps) for 48h. After ~36h, a single request that required a large workspace (long sequence length) triggered OOM.
- nvidia-smi during timeline: overall used memory mostly constant but there are spikes when large workspace allocations happen; after the spike, free memory does not fully return to baseline.
- cuMemGetInfo check from our runtime: free memory reported smaller than nvidia-smi by ~100MB intermittently.
- After restarting the process, memory availability returns to expected baseline and workloads succeed.
- Enabling CUDA caching allocator (cudaMallocAsync / memory pool) reduced frequency of OOMs in experiments but did not completely eliminate them.

Profiling and tools used:
- nvidia-smi sampling (10s cadence) for long-running trend.
- Nsight Systems traces for request that failed with OOM to capture API-level allocation calls and timelines.
- Custom logging in runtime for every cudaMalloc/cudaFree size and timestamp (aggregated per-request).
- cuMemGetInfo sampling before/after model load and during request processing.
- Linux /proc/<pid>/status + pmap for host-side allocations pinned via cudaHostAlloc.
- GPU debug tools: CUDA memory pool debug flags and environment variables (CUDA_MALLOC_ASYNC_POOL_SIZE_MB, CUDA_MEMPOOL_REUSE_ALLOCATION, etc.)

Key allocator behavior findings:
- We saw many small allocations (~<1MB) created frequently during tokenization and auxiliary ops; free lists were heavily utilized.
- Large temporary workspace allocations (10s-100s MB) for matmul/GEMM and attention kernels sometimes required contiguous regions that did not exist due to fragmentation. The allocator attempts to fall back to cudaMalloc and fails because largest contiguous free block < request size despite total free memory being sufficient.
- cudaFree latencies observed: some cudaFree calls took >50ms when invoked concurrently across threads, increasing the chance of overlapping allocation requests and races.
- The host-side caching allocator (our layer) returns freed blocks to a cache for reuse; however, edge case patterns where varied sizes are requested leads to cache churn and ineffective reuse, exacerbating fragmentation.

Specific interactions:
- cuBLAS/cuDNN: They allocate internal workspaces on demand; sizes change with sequence length and batch size. If they request a workspace larger than any single free span, OOM occurs.
- KV cache: we observed incremental growth due to incremental keys being materialized; when combined with transient workspace allocations, worst-case peak exceeded available largest contiguous region.
- cudaMallocAsync/memory pool: when enabled with a sufficiently sized pool, fragmentation is reduced because the pool services small allocations from a contiguous backing allocation. But incorrect pool sizing or not setting the pool to encompass peak concurrency still permits OOM.

Experiments and results:
- Baseline: default allocator (cudaMalloc/cudaFree) -> OOM ~36h in stress run.
- Enable caching allocator (our host caching + cudaMallocAsync with 16GB pool) -> OOMs reduced but still found on stress with large rare workspace requests.
- Force periodic allocator compaction (restart/pool reset every 24h) -> mitigates but is not acceptable operationally.
- Harmonize workspace sizes across model variants (cap max workspace requested by kernels with fallback slower kernel) -> eliminated observed OOM in 72h run but caused ~8-12% latency regression for some requests.
- Implemented best-fit bucketed allocator for transient small buffers -> reduced small-block fragmentation metrics by ~60%.

Working root cause conclusion (current):
- Primary driver is fragmentation of physical GPU memory due to mixture of allocation sizes and lifetime patterns (persistent KV cache + frequent small ephemeral allocations + occasional very large workspace allocations). The allocator (legacy cudaMalloc/cudaFree or insufficiently sized cudaMallocAsync pool) can report insufficient contiguous memory even when the aggregate free capacity is adequate.
- Secondary contributors: non-deterministic cudaFree latencies and interleaving of third-party library allocations in multi-threaded request handling.

Mitigations (short-term):
- Enable cudaMallocAsync/memory pool with pool size configured to cover expected peak working set plus headroom. Document env vars and make default config in Dedicated and Private deployments.
- Reduce max workspace requested by kernels via algorithmic fallbacks or capped workspace parameter; add explicit kernel selection path for memory-constrained hosts.
- Add periodic memory pool trimming + safe compaction hooks (best-effort) when we detect fragmentation approaching threshold.
- Add runtime guard: on repeated allocation failures, attempt to trigger memory pool reset and retry allocation path before returning OOM to client (safely serialized).

Mitigations (medium-term):
- Implement and upstream an internal memory manager that: uses a best-fit bucketed pool for small allocs, reserves contiguous large slabs for big workspace allocations, and isolates KV cache into its own reserved pool.
- Change request scheduling to avoid concurrent large-workspace allocations when memory pressure is high (admission control or token-bucket for large-workspace requests).
- Improve visibility: expose time-series of largest free contiguous block size (via cuMemGetInfo + scanning our internal free-lists) to Console so users can diagnose fragmentation vs total capacity issues.

Operational recommendations / runbook snippets:
- On OOM incidents: collect nsight trace + runtime cudaMalloc/cudaFree logs, dump cuMemGetInfo sample, note concurrent batch sizes and sequence lengths. If restart fixes, document time-to-failure and check for pattern.
- For Dedicated fleet: proactively enable memory pools and set pool size per instance type (A100-40GB -> pool 36GB leave headroom for driver and persistence).
- Add alerting on fragmentation metric: fraction of total free memory residing in blocks < 32MB and largest contiguous free block < required workspace threshold.

Open questions / TODOs:
- Determine exact behavior of third-party libs: can we force cuDNN/cuBLAS to use our memory pool APIs reliably in all versions we support? (Action: Miguel to validate on CUDA 11.7/11.8/12.x).
- What is the best default pool sizing heuristic for mixed workloads (chat + embeddings + reranking)? (Action: Priya to create workload-based sizing experiment).
- Can we safely garbage collect or compact KV cache entries when fragmentation crosses thresholds without harming correctness and latency? (Action: Jonah investigate tradeoffs).
- Add unit/integration tests to reproduce fragmentation reliably in CI (synthetic workload generator that issues interleaved small and large allocations).

Appendix: quick commands used during investigation:
- nvidia-smi --query-gpu=memory.total,memory.used --format=csv -l 10
- python script: sample cuMemGetInfo before/after request + log cudaMalloc/cudaFree sizes (attached in linked PR)
- Nsight Systems: nsys profile --sample=cpu --trace=cuda,osrt --output=oom-investigation

Notes to self: capture thresholds and configs we converge on into "serving-runtime/default-memory-pools" config and add a README for operators.
